builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
summary: Replaces round-to-nearest quantization of FP32 shadow weights to BF16 with stochastic rounding during RL post-training. Costs are limited to a modified quantization step and added implementation complexity, with no stated memory or latency overhead. It can fail if the implementation does not reproduce the claimed convergence or KL benefits on the reader's specific model, dataset, and training stack.
rationale: The method targets a real BF16 convergence bottleneck in RL fine-tuning, but its benefit should be validated on the reader's own workload before adoption.
technique: Stochastic rounding for BF16 shadow weights in RL post-training

claims.statement: Replaces round-to-nearest quantization of FP32 shadow weights to BF16 with stochastic rounding during RL post-training. Costs are limited to a modified quantization step and added implementation complexity, with no stated memory or latency overhead. It can fail if the implementation does not reproduce the claimed convergence or KL benefits on the reader's specific model, dataset, and training stack.
Matches FP16 convergence speed in RL with verifiable rewards while retaining BF16's FP32-like dynamic range and reducing KL divergence relative to higher-learning-rate BF16 training.
